Sheet Metal vs CNC Machining: How to Choose the Right Method for Your Metal Parts Quick Answer: Choose sheet metal for uniform-thickness enclosures, panels, and formed brackets when bends and production volume support lower unit cost. Choose CNC machining for variable wall thickness, precision bores, tight feature relationships, and complex 3D geometry. Use a hybrid design when a formed structure needs precision-machined interfaces. A quote comes back for a bracket, and it's priced as a CNC part — machined from solid aluminum, a few hours of spindle time, a per-part cost that makes sense for ten units but starts looking painful at a thousand. The same bracket, cut and bent from sheet stock, would cost a fraction of that at volume. Nobody made a mistake here; the part just got quoted through the wrong process for its actual requirements. That mismatch — sheet metal work priced and built like a machined part, or vice versa — is one of the more expensive mistakes in early product design, and it's usually avoidable with a clear framework for which process actually fits. The Core Difference Sheet metal fabrication forms a part from flat stock — cutting, bending, and joining thin material into its final shape. CNC machining removes material from a solid block until the final geometry emerges. That distinction — forming versus removing — is what drives almost every practical difference between the two: cost structure, achievable geometry, tolerance, and how each scales with volume. It's also why the two processes don't compete on a level playing field for most parts — once you know which side of "form vs. remove" your part naturally sits on, half the decision is already made before cost even enters the conversation. CNC or Sheet Metal — We Do Both Need CNC and Sheet Metal? We've Got Both JLCCNC does both CNC machining and sheet metal fabrication in-house. Upload your file, get an instant quote. Get Instant Quote Decision Framework Factor Favors Sheet Metal Favors CNC Machining Wall thickness Uniform, thin — typically under 6mm, though this depends on material and forming method Variable thickness, thick sections Geometry Flat panels, bent enclosures, brackets Complex 3D features, pockets, threaded bosses Tolerance ±0.1–0.3mm typical, tighter with secondary operations ±0.01–0.05mm achievable, depending on material and feature size Material waste Low — forming generates minimal scrap Higher — material is cut away as chips Volume economics Cost drops fast with volume, but the rate depends heavily on whether the process is press-brake bending or stamping Cost scales more linearly with volume Prototype cost Can be higher per-unit at very low volume due to setup Often cheaper for true one-offs (no tooling needed) Lead time Faster once in production; batch-dependent Often faster for a single prototype, no setup to plan around Surface finish out of process Generally rougher without secondary finishing, though this varies by material and process Can achieve fine finish directly off the tool The numbers above are typical ranges, not guarantees — actual tolerance and thickness limits depend on the specific material, part size, forming or cutting method, and feature geometry involved. Neither column is "better" in the abstract — the right answer depends entirely on which factors matter for a specific part. How to Choose: A 5-Step Decision Tree The table above tells you what each process is generally good at. This turns that into something you can actually run a part through: Is wall thickness uniform across the part? If yes, sheet metal is still in play. If the part needs varying thickness in different sections, that alone usually rules sheet metal out. Can the geometry be formed by bending, rather than requiring it be cut from solid? A flat pattern that folds into the final shape favors sheet metal. A shape with internal pockets, bosses, or geometry that can't unfold flat needs machining. Does any feature need a precision bore, bearing seat, or tightly toleranced hole relationship? If yes, that feature — and possibly the whole part — needs CNC, even if the rest of the geometry would otherwise suit sheet metal. Where does your volume sit? Low volume with simple geometry often favors CNC (no tooling, no bend planning). Moderate-to-high volume with sheet-metal-compatible geometry usually favors sheet metal. Does the part actually need to be one piece, or could it be a hybrid? If step 3 flagged a precision feature but the rest of the part is sheet-metal-friendly, a hybrid assembly is often cheaper than machining the whole thing. Running an actual part through these five questions in order, rather than defaulting to whichever process a designer is more familiar with, is usually enough to catch a mismatch before it turns into a bad quote. Where Sheet Metal Wins Enclosures, panels, brackets, and chassis with mostly uniform wall thickness are sheet metal's home turf. A sheet metal enclosure that would need a solid block of aluminum hollowed out on a mill costs dramatically more in both material and machine time than the same shape cut flat and folded into a box. At production volume, this gap widens further — sheet metal's low scrap rate and fast cycle time on simple bends make it the clear cost winner for parts that don't need machining's tighter tolerances or 3D complexity. There are design rules that come with this territory, and they're worth knowing before a part gets drawn rather than after it comes back from the shop with a note attached. Holes placed too close to a bend line will distort during forming — a rough rule of thumb is keeping at least 3x the material thickness between a hole's edge and the bend line. Minimum bend radius matters too: pushing a bend tighter than the material can reasonably take leads to cracking on the outer surface, especially with harder alloys. These aren't limitations that make sheet metal a lesser option — they're just the constraints that come with forming instead of removing material, and designing around them from the start avoids a redesign cycle later. Our sheet metal design guidelines go deeper into these bend, hole-spacing, and flange rules if you're drawing a part now. Where CNC Machining Wins Anything needing tight tolerances, threaded holes machined directly into the part, varying wall thickness, or complex 3D features that can't be formed from flat stock belongs in CNC machining. A mounting plate needing precisely located, tightly toleranced holes for a bearing assembly isn't a sheet metal job — the tolerance and feature complexity simply exceed what forming can reliably produce. Deep features have their own limits worth knowing on the machining side. A pocket deeper than roughly four times its diameter starts requiring longer, more flexible tooling, which drives up cycle time and cost, and increases the risk of chatter or tool deflection affecting the finish. It doesn't rule the feature out — it just changes the cost math, and it's another reason "can CNC do it" and "should CNC do it at this price point" are different questions. For true one-off prototypes, machining is also often cheaper in practice, since it needs no tooling investment the way some sheet metal processes — stamping in particular — do. Standard press-brake bending, the default for custom and low-volume sheet metal work, doesn't carry that same tooling penalty; it's cutting and forming operations, not a stamping die, which is why a low-volume bracket cut on a laser and folded on a brake can still compete with machining on price even without any tooling amortized into it. Cost Drivers, Not Just Volume Volume matters, but it's not the whole cost story — and treating "sheet metal wins at volume" as the entire rule misses where the actual cost comes from on each side. On the sheet metal side , cost is driven by material utilization (how efficiently the flat pattern nests on the sheet), the number of cuts and bends, whether parts need welding or additional fastening, and any secondary surface finishing. A part with a simple flat pattern and two bends costs very differently from one with a dozen tabs, slots, and a welded seam — even at the same volume and material. On the CNC side , cost tracks the size of the starting stock, how much material has to be removed to reach final geometry, how many times the part needs to be re-fixtured to reach all its features, tooling wear on harder materials, and how tightly toleranced features need inspecting after the cut. A part that looks simple but needs machining from six sides costs more than its footprint suggests, regardless of order quantity. This is also where the sheet metal tooling question matters. Laser cutting and press-brake bending — the default route for prototypes and low-to-moderate volume custom sheet metal — carry no tooling cost; you're paying for cutting and setup time per batch. Stamping, by contrast, requires a dedicated die, which is a real upfront cost that only pays off once volume is high enough to amortize it across thousands of parts. Comparing a stamped-part cost curve to a CNC part is a different conversation than comparing a laser-cut-and-bent part to a CNC part, and conflating the two is a common source of quotes that don't match expectations. Tolerance and Feature Reality Check Some features have a real answer on which process they need, and it's worth being direct about which ones: bearing bores, features requiring tight coaxiality between two holes, precisely located dowel or locating pin holes, and complex internal cavities are CNC territory. Sheet metal forming doesn't hold that level of geometric precision, and no amount of secondary finishing changes that. But it's a mistake to jump straight to "this part needs a thread, so it needs CNC." Sheet metal has its own ways of handling fasteners and threaded connections without machining the whole part: bent tabs with clearance holes, PEM self-clinching fasteners pressed into the sheet, riveted nuts, or welded studs all add threaded or fastening points to a sheet metal part without requiring the part itself be machined. The real question isn't "does this need a thread" — it's "does this need a machined thread in solid material, or would a pressed-in fastener do the job." Most bracket and enclosure fastening needs fall into the second category. Redesigning a Machined Part for Sheet Metal This is often the highest-value move in the whole decision, and it's the one that's easy to miss when a part starts life as a CNC drawing and never gets reconsidered. If a part is currently machined but doesn't actually need machining's precision everywhere, redesigning it around sheet metal can cut cost meaningfully at volume. A few principles that tend to work: Unify wall thickness. A machined part with varying wall thickness for structural reasons can often be redesigned around a single uniform thickness plus added ribs or folded flanges for stiffness, opening the door to sheet metal. Replace pocketed/hollowed sections with a folded shell. A block that's mostly hollowed out to save weight is, functionally, often just an enclosure — which is exactly what sheet metal is good at forming instead of removing material to create. Use flanges and fasteners instead of solid thick walls. Where a machined part relies on thick material for mounting strength, a folded flange with the right fastener often does the same structural job at a fraction of the material cost. Keep precision interfaces as small, separate CNC parts. The redesign doesn't have to eliminate machining entirely — isolating the one feature that genuinely needs tight tolerance into a small machined insert, bolted or riveted into a sheet metal shell, usually costs less than machining the whole part just to get that one feature right. One Hybrid Assembly Example Plenty of real products aren't a clean either/or. A sheet metal chassis provides the lightweight, cost-effective structural shell, while CNC-machined brackets or mounting plates handle the specific spots that need tight tolerances a formed part can't hold — bolted or riveted into the sheet metal structure. A common version of this: a sheet-metal chassis with a CNC-machined bearing bracket bolted into it. The chassis handles the overall shape, mounting points, and structural panel work — all things sheet metal does well and cheaply at volume. The bearing bracket needs a precisely bored, tightly toleranced hole to seat a bearing correctly, which sheet metal forming can't reliably hold. Rather than machining the entire chassis to get that one bore right, the bore lives on a small dedicated machined part, and the two interfaces — chassis mounting holes and bracket mounting holes — are designed to align during assembly. This hybrid approach is common enough in electronics and equipment housings that it's worth considering from the start of a design, rather than defaulting to one process and forcing every feature to fit it. It's also one of the more practical reasons to source both processes from the same shop — fewer handoffs, fewer tolerance mismatches between the two parts when they're meant to bolt together. Our enclosure design guide goes deeper into this specific decision for enclosure design — covering the same choice this article addresses, but focused on the practical challenges of enclosure geometry, internal component fit, and assembly. Material Considerations The two processes don't just differ in how they shape metal — they differ in which metals are practical to work with, and that's often the deciding factor before cost or geometry even get discussed. Aluminum 5052 forms well and is a workhorse for sheet metal enclosures, but it's a softer alloy that machines less cleanly at tight tolerances than harder grades. Aluminum 6061 is the opposite pattern: it machines cleanly and holds tolerance well on a CNC part, but its formability is more limited — tight bend radii in 6061 are more prone to cracking than in 5052. 304 and 201 stainless steel both fabricate well as sheet metal for enclosures and structural panels, but on the machining side stainless work-hardens as it's cut, which means slower feeds, more tool wear, and a costlier part than the same geometry in aluminum or steel. Cold rolled steel is a common, economical choice for sheet metal work and machines acceptably too, which is part of why it shows up so often in both processes for general-purpose brackets and housings. If a design is locked into a specific alloy for strength, corrosion resistance, or cost reasons, it's worth checking that alloy's behavior in the process you're leaning toward before finalizing — a great geometry choice can still get expensive if the material fights the process. See our guide to sheet metal material types for a fuller breakdown by alloy. The Real Cost Curve The mismatch described at the top of this article — a bracket quoted as CNC when sheet metal would've been dramatically cheaper at volume — happens because the two processes' cost curves cross at different points depending on the part. At very low volume (a handful of prototypes), the two are often close, sometimes with machining even edging ahead since sheet metal's setup costs don't amortize yet. As volume grows, sheet metal's per-part cost typically drops well below machining's for parts within its geometric capability — since machining cost stays tied to cutting time and material removed no matter how many parts you order, while sheet metal's setup cost gets spread across a growing batch. Exactly where that crossover happens shifts with the factors above; a simple two-bend bracket crosses over earlier than a part needing several welds and a finish operation. Push volume high enough and the gap widens further for simple flat-and-bend geometries, though a part with genuinely complex 3D features may never cross over — sheet metal simply can't produce it at any volume, which makes the "geometry first, cost second" ordering of this decision worth sticking to. See our breakdown of CNC machining costs for more on how machining cost is actually built up. A Common Mistake Worth Flagging Choosing a process based on which one a designer is more familiar with, rather than which one actually fits the part, is a frequent and costly habit. An engineer used to specifying machined parts sometimes defaults to CNC even for a simple bent bracket that sheet metal would produce at a fraction of the cost — not from any real requirement, just familiarity. Running through the decision factors and the 5-step tree above explicitly, rather than defaulting to habit, is a genuinely cheap way to avoid overpaying on a part that didn't need machining's capability in the first place. FAQ Is sheet metal fabrication always cheaper than CNC machining? Not always — at very low volume the two can be close, and for parts needing tight tolerances or complex 3D geometry, machining is often the only option regardless of cost. Sheet metal's cost advantage grows most clearly at moderate-to-high volume for parts within its geometric capability. Can a part be redesigned to use sheet metal instead of machining to save cost? Often, yes — if the part's function doesn't actually require variable thickness or fine 3D features, redesigning around uniform-thickness formed geometry can meaningfully cut cost, especially at volume. This is worth evaluating during design review rather than after tooling or a first production run. What tolerance can sheet metal fabrication achieve? Typical sheet metal tolerances run around ±0.1–0.3mm depending on the process and material thickness — tighter than many people assume, but still generally looser than CNC machining's ±0.01–0.05mm capability. Which process has a faster lead time? It depends on where you are in the product cycle. For a single prototype, CNC machining often turns around faster since there's no tooling or bend planning involved. Once you're ordering in batches, sheet metal generally catches up and can move faster per part, since cycle times on cutting and bending are short compared to machining time per unit. Do sheet metal and CNC machined parts ever get combined in one assembly? Yes, commonly — a sheet metal structure (enclosure, chassis) paired with CNC-machined components at the specific points needing tight tolerance is a standard approach, especially in electronics and equipment housings. Does material choice limit which process I can use? Not usually as a hard limit, but it changes the cost and quality picture. Softer, more formable alloys like 5052 aluminum favor sheet metal; harder alloys and stainless steel machine well but form less easily, and stainless in particular gets more expensive to machine due to work-hardening during cutting. Can sheet metal parts use threaded fasteners? Yes — without machining a thread into solid material. PEM self-clinching nuts, riveted nuts, and welded studs are the standard ways to add a threaded connection point to a sheet metal part, and they're usually cheaper than machining a thread would be on an equivalent solid section. When does stamping change the cost comparison? Stamping requires a dedicated die, which is a real upfront tooling cost that only pays off at high volume — typically thousands of parts. Below that, laser cutting and press-brake bending (no tooling cost) is the more relevant sheet metal comparison against CNC, not stamping. Can sheet metal meet a ±0.05 mm requirement? Generally no, not directly out of the forming process — sheet metal tolerances typically run ±0.1–0.3mm. A feature genuinely needing ±0.05mm should be isolated to a CNC-machined component, even within an otherwise sheet-metal part or assembly. Note: tolerance and thickness figures throughout are typical ranges. Actual achievable tolerance depends on material, part size, and process — confirm against your specific part with an engineering review before finalizing a design. Whether your part is a better fit for sheet metal or CNC machining often comes down to details that are easy to miss on a drawing alone — tolerance requirements, wall thickness consistency, or where your volume actually sits on the cost curve. Sheet Metal vs CNC Machining: How to Choose the Right Method for Your Metal Parts Quick Answer: Choose sheet metal for uniform-thickness enclosures, panels, and formed brackets when bends and production volume support lower unit cost. Choose CNC machining for variable wall thickness, precision bores, tight feature relationships, and complex 3D geometry. Use a hybrid design when a formed structure needs precision-machined interfaces. A quote comes back for a bracket, and it's priced as a CNC part — machined from solid aluminum, a few hours of spindle time, a per-part cost that makes sense for ten units but starts looking painful at a thousand. The same bracket, cut and bent from sheet stock, would cost a fraction of that at volume. Nobody made a mistake here; the part just got quoted through the wrong process for its actual requirements. That mismatch — sheet metal work priced and built like a machined part, or vice versa — is one of the more expensive mistakes in early product design, and it's usually avoidable with a clear framework for which process actually fits. The Core Difference Sheet metal fabrication forms a part from flat stock — cutting, bending, and joining thin material into its final shape. CNC machining removes material from a solid block until the final geometry emerges. That distinction — forming versus removing — is what drives almost every practical difference between the two: cost structure, achievable geometry, tolerance, and how each scales with volume. It's also why the two processes don't compete on a level playing field for most parts — once you know which side of "form vs. remove" your part naturally sits on, half the decision is already made before cost even enters the conversation. Get Instant Quote Decision Framework Factor Favors Sheet Metal Favors CNC Machining Wall thickness Uniform, thin — typically under 6mm, though this depends on material and forming method Variable thickness, thick sections Geometry Flat panels, bent enclosures, brackets Complex 3D features, pockets, threaded bosses Tolerance ±0.1–0.3mm typical, tighter with secondary operations ±0.01–0.05mm achievable, depending on material and feature size Material waste Low — forming generates minimal scrap Higher — material is cut away as chips Volume economics Cost drops fast with volume, but the rate depends heavily on whether the process is press-brake bending or stamping Cost scales more linearly with volume Prototype cost Can be higher per-unit at very low volume due to setup Often cheaper for true one-offs (no tooling needed) Lead time Faster once in production; batch-dependent Often faster for a single prototype, no setup to plan around Surface finish out of process Generally rougher without secondary finishing, though this varies by material and process Can achieve fine finish directly off the tool The numbers above are typical ranges, not guarantees — actual tolerance and thickness limits depend on the specific material, part size, forming or cutting method, and feature geometry involved. Neither column is "better" in the abstract — the right answer depends entirely on which factors matter for a specific part. How to Choose: A 5-Step Decision Tree The table above tells you what each process is generally good at. This turns that into something you can actually run a part through: Is wall thickness uniform across the part? If yes, sheet metal is still in play. If the part needs varying thickness in different sections, that alone usually rules sheet metal out. Can the geometry be formed by bending, rather than requiring it be cut from solid? A flat pattern that folds into the final shape favors sheet metal. A shape with internal pockets, bosses, or geometry that can't unfold flat needs machining. Does any feature need a precision bore, bearing seat, or tightly toleranced hole relationship? If yes, that feature — and possibly the whole part — needs CNC, even if the rest of the geometry would otherwise suit sheet metal. Where does your volume sit? Low volume with simple geometry often favors CNC (no tooling, no bend planning). Moderate-to-high volume with sheet-metal-compatible geometry usually favors sheet metal. Does the part actually need to be one piece, or could it be a hybrid? If step 3 flagged a precision feature but the rest of the part is sheet-metal-friendly, a hybrid assembly is often cheaper than machining the whole thing. Running an actual part through these five questions in order, rather than defaulting to whichever process a designer is more familiar with, is usually enough to catch a mismatch before it turns into a bad quote. Where Sheet Metal Wins Enclosures, panels, brackets, and chassis with mostly uniform wall thickness are sheet metal's home turf. A sheet metal enclosure that would need a solid block of aluminum hollowed out on a mill costs dramatically more in both material and machine time than the same shape cut flat and folded into a box. At production volume, this gap widens further — sheet metal's low scrap rate and fast cycle time on simple bends make it the clear cost winner for parts that don't need machining's tighter tolerances or 3D complexity. There are design rules that come with this territory, and they're worth knowing before a part gets drawn rather than after it comes back from the shop with a note attached. Holes placed too close to a bend line will distort during forming — a rough rule of thumb is keeping at least 3x the material thickness between a hole's edge and the bend line. Minimum bend radius matters too: pushing a bend tighter than the material can reasonably take leads to cracking on the outer surface, especially with harder alloys. These aren't limitations that make sheet metal a lesser option — they're just the constraints that come with forming instead of removing material, and designing around them from the start avoids a redesign cycle later. Our sheet metal design guidelines go deeper into these bend, hole-spacing, and flange rules if you're drawing a part now. Where CNC Machining Wins Anything needing tight tolerances, threaded holes machined directly into the part, varying wall thickness, or complex 3D features that can't be formed from flat stock belongs in CNC machining. A mounting plate needing precisely located, tightly toleranced holes for a bearing assembly isn't a sheet metal job — the tolerance and feature complexity simply exceed what forming can reliably produce. Deep features have their own limits worth knowing on the machining side. A pocket deeper than roughly four times its diameter starts requiring longer, more flexible tooling, which drives up cycle time and cost, and increases the risk of chatter or tool deflection affecting the finish. It doesn't rule the feature out — it just changes the cost math, and it's another reason "can CNC do it" and "should CNC do it at this price point" are different questions. For true one-off prototypes, machining is also often cheaper in practice, since it needs no tooling investment the way some sheet metal processes — stamping in particular — do. Standard press-brake bending, the default for custom and low-volume sheet metal work, doesn't carry that same tooling penalty; it's cutting and forming operations, not a stamping die, which is why a low-volume bracket cut on a laser and folded on a brake can still compete with machining on price even without any tooling amortized into it. Cost Drivers, Not Just Volume Volume matters, but it's not the whole cost story — and treating "sheet metal wins at volume" as the entire rule misses where the actual cost comes from on each side. On the sheet metal side , cost is driven by material utilization (how efficiently the flat pattern nests on the sheet), the number of cuts and bends, whether parts need welding or additional fastening, and any secondary surface finishing. A part with a simple flat pattern and two bends costs very differently from one with a dozen tabs, slots, and a welded seam — even at the same volume and material. On the CNC side , cost tracks the size of the starting stock, how much material has to be removed to reach final geometry, how many times the part needs to be re-fixtured to reach all its features, tooling wear on harder materials, and how tightly toleranced features need inspecting after the cut. A part that looks simple but needs machining from six sides costs more than its footprint suggests, regardless of order quantity. This is also where the sheet metal tooling question matters. Laser cutting and press-brake bending — the default route for prototypes and low-to-moderate volume custom sheet metal — carry no tooling cost; you're paying for cutting and setup time per batch. Stamping, by contrast, requires a dedicated die, which is a real upfront cost that only pays off once volume is high enough to amortize it across thousands of parts. Comparing a stamped-part cost curve to a CNC part is a different conversation than comparing a laser-cut-and-bent part to a CNC part, and conflating the two is a common source of quotes that don't match expectations. Tolerance and Feature Reality Check Some features have a real answer on which process they need, and it's worth being direct about which ones: bearing bores, features requiring tight coaxiality between two holes, precisely located dowel or locating pin holes, and complex internal cavities are CNC territory. Sheet metal forming doesn't hold that level of geometric precision, and no amount of secondary finishing changes that. But it's a mistake to jump straight to "this part needs a thread, so it needs CNC." Sheet metal has its own ways of handling fasteners and threaded connections without machining the whole part: bent tabs with clearance holes, PEM self-clinching fasteners pressed into the sheet, riveted nuts, or welded studs all add threaded or fastening points to a sheet metal part without requiring the part itself be machined. The real question isn't "does this need a thread" — it's "does this need a machined thread in solid material, or would a pressed-in fastener do the job." Most bracket and enclosure fastening needs fall into the second category. Redesigning a Machined Part for Sheet Metal This is often the highest-value move in the whole decision, and it's the one that's easy to miss when a part starts life as a CNC drawing and never gets reconsidered. If a part is currently machined but doesn't actually need machining's precision everywhere, redesigning it around sheet metal can cut cost meaningfully at volume. A few principles that tend to work: Unify wall thickness. A machined part with varying wall thickness for structural reasons can often be redesigned around a single uniform thickness plus added ribs or folded flanges for stiffness, opening the door to sheet metal. Replace pocketed/hollowed sections with a folded shell. A block that's mostly hollowed out to save weight is, functionally, often just an enclosure — which is exactly what sheet metal is good at forming instead of removing material to create. Use flanges and fasteners instead of solid thick walls. Where a machined part relies on thick material for mounting strength, a folded flange with the right fastener often does the same structural job at a fraction of the material cost. Keep precision interfaces as small, separate CNC parts. The redesign doesn't have to eliminate machining entirely — isolating the one feature that genuinely needs tight tolerance into a small machined insert, bolted or riveted into a sheet metal shell, usually costs less than machining the whole part just to get that one feature right. One Hybrid Assembly Example Plenty of real products aren't a clean either/or. A sheet metal chassis provides the lightweight, cost-effective structural shell, while CNC-machined brackets or mounting plates handle the specific spots that need tight tolerances a formed part can't hold — bolted or riveted into the sheet metal structure. A common version of this: a sheet-metal chassis with a CNC-machined bearing bracket bolted into it. The chassis handles the overall shape, mounting points, and structural panel work — all things sheet metal does well and cheaply at volume. The bearing bracket needs a precisely bored, tightly toleranced hole to seat a bearing correctly, which sheet metal forming can't reliably hold. Rather than machining the entire chassis to get that one bore right, the bore lives on a small dedicated machined part, and the two interfaces — chassis mounting holes and bracket mounting holes — are designed to align during assembly. This hybrid approach is common enough in electronics and equipment housings that it's worth considering from the start of a design, rather than defaulting to one process and forcing every feature to fit it. It's also one of the more practical reasons to source both processes from the same shop — fewer handoffs, fewer tolerance mismatches between the two parts when they're meant to bolt together. Our enclosure design guide goes deeper into this specific decision for enclosure design — covering the same choice this article addresses, but focused on the practical challenges of enclosure geometry, internal component fit, and assembly. Material Considerations The two processes don't just differ in how they shape metal — they differ in which metals are practical to work with, and that's often the deciding factor before cost or geometry even get discussed. Aluminum 5052 forms well and is a workhorse for sheet metal enclosures, but it's a softer alloy that machines less cleanly at tight tolerances than harder grades. Aluminum 6061 is the opposite pattern: it machines cleanly and holds tolerance well on a CNC part, but its formability is more limited — tight bend radii in 6061 are more prone to cracking than in 5052. 304 and 201 stainless steel both fabricate well as sheet metal for enclosures and structural panels, but on the machining side stainless work-hardens as it's cut, which means slower feeds, more tool wear, and a costlier part than the same geometry in aluminum or steel. Cold rolled steel is a common, economical choice for sheet metal work and machines acceptably too, which is part of why it shows up so often in both processes for general-purpose brackets and housings. If a design is locked into a specific alloy for strength, corrosion resistance, or cost reasons, it's worth checking that alloy's behavior in the process you're leaning toward before finalizing — a great geometry choice can still get expensive if the material fights the process. See our guide to sheet metal material types for a fuller breakdown by alloy. The Real Cost Curve The mismatch described at the top of this article — a bracket quoted as CNC when sheet metal would've been dramatically cheaper at volume — happens because the two processes' cost curves cross at different points depending on the part. At very low volume (a handful of prototypes), the two are often close, sometimes with machining even edging ahead since sheet metal's setup costs don't amortize yet. As volume grows, sheet metal's per-part cost typically drops well below machining's for parts within its geometric capability — since machining cost stays tied to cutting time and material removed no matter how many parts you order, while sheet metal's setup cost gets spread across a growing batch. Exactly where that crossover happens shifts with the factors above; a simple two-bend bracket crosses over earlier than a part needing several welds and a finish operation. Push volume high enough and the gap widens further for simple flat-and-bend geometries, though a part with genuinely complex 3D features may never cross over — sheet metal simply can't produce it at any volume, which makes the "geometry first, cost second" ordering of this decision worth sticking to. See our breakdown of CNC machining costs for more on how machining cost is actually built up. A Common Mistake Worth Flagging Choosing a process based on which one a designer is more familiar with, rather than which one actually fits the part, is a frequent and costly habit. An engineer used to specifying machined parts sometimes defaults to CNC even for a simple bent bracket that sheet metal would produce at a fraction of the cost — not from any real requirement, just familiarity. Running through the decision factors and the 5-step tree above explicitly, rather than defaulting to habit, is a genuinely cheap way to avoid overpaying on a part that didn't need machining's capability in the first place. FAQ Is sheet metal fabrication always cheaper than CNC machining? Not always — at very low volume the two can be close, and for parts needing tight tolerances or complex 3D geometry, machining is often the only option regardless of cost. Sheet metal's cost advantage grows most clearly at moderate-to-high volume for parts within its geometric capability. Can a part be redesigned to use sheet metal instead of machining to save cost? Often, yes — if the part's function doesn't actually require variable thickness or fine 3D features, redesigning around uniform-thickness formed geometry can meaningfully cut cost, especially at volume. This is worth evaluating during design review rather than after tooling or a first production run. What tolerance can sheet metal fabrication achieve? Typical sheet metal tolerances run around ±0.1–0.3mm depending on the process and material thickness — tighter than many people assume, but still generally looser than CNC machining's ±0.01–0.05mm capability. Which process has a faster lead time? It depends on where you are in the product cycle. For a single prototype, CNC machining often turns around faster since there's no tooling or bend planning involved. Once you're ordering in batches, sheet metal generally catches up and can move faster per part, since cycle times on cutting and bending are short compared to machining time per unit. Do sheet metal and CNC machined parts ever get combined in one assembly? Yes, commonly — a sheet metal structure (enclosure, chassis) paired with CNC-machined components at the specific points needing tight tolerance is a standard approach, especially in electronics and equipment housings. Does material choice limit which process I can use? Not usually as a hard limit, but it changes the cost and quality picture. Softer, more formable alloys like 5052 aluminum favor sheet metal; harder alloys and stainless steel machine well but form less easily, and stainless in particular gets more expensive to machine due to work-hardening during cutting. Can sheet metal parts use threaded fasteners? Yes — without machining a thread into solid material. PEM self-clinching nuts, riveted nuts, and welded studs are the standard ways to add a threaded connection point to a sheet metal part, and they're usually cheaper than machining a thread would be on an equivalent solid section. When does stamping change the cost comparison? Stamping requires a dedicated die, which is a real upfront tooling cost that only pays off at high volume — typically thousands of parts. Below that, laser cutting and press-brake bending (no tooling cost) is the more relevant sheet metal comparison against CNC, not stamping. Can sheet metal meet a ±0.05 mm requirement? Generally no, not directly out of the forming process — sheet metal tolerances typically run ±0.1–0.3mm. A feature genuinely needing ±0.05mm should be isolated to a CNC-machined component, even within an otherwise sheet-metal part or assembly. Note: tolerance and thickness figures throughout are typical ranges. Actual achievable tolerance depends on material, part size, and process — confirm against your specific part with an engineering review before finalizing a design. Not Sure Which Process Fits Your Part? Whether your part is a better fit for sheet metal or CNC machining often comes down to details that are easy to miss on a drawing alone — tolerance requirements, wall thickness consistency, or where your volume actually sits on the cost curve. Published Jul 30, 2025, updated Jul 28, 2025 5 min Threading a hole sounds simple, until you’re deciding between thread milling and tapping . Both methods are staples in CNC machining and manual operations, but they serve different purposes, machines, and tolerances. Whether you're threading aluminum, stainless steel, or titanium, choosing the wrong method can mean broken tools, scrapped parts, or wasted hours. Let’s break down the real differences between thread milling vs tapping , when to use one over the other, and how to choose the right tool for your part. What is Tapping? Tapping is the traditional method of creating internal threads by driving a tap, a hardened cutting tool, into a pre-drilled hole. It’s fast, easy to set up, and widely used in manual and CNC operations. There are three common types of taps: ● Hand taps – used manually with a T-handle ● Spiral point taps – best for through holes ● Spiral flute taps – best for blind holes Taps are typically specific to one thread size and pitch, which makes them convenient but rigid in flexibility. What is Thread Milling? Thread milling , on the other hand, uses a rotating tool called a thread mill to cut threads with a helical interpolation motion. The tool enters the hole and follows a spiral path to form the thread, using a CNC program to control pitch and depth. There are three types of thread mills: ● Single-point thread mills – extremely flexible for custom threads ● Multi-form thread mills – cut the full profile in one pass ● Indexable thread mills – ideal for large threads or production runs Thread milling may require more programming and setup time, but it shines in areas tapping simply can't reach. Thread Milling vs Tapping: Head-to-Head Comparison Let’s stack up thread milling vs tapping in the areas that matter most: Feature Tapping Thread Milling Speed Faster for high-volume production Slower, especially for large threads Tool Flexibility One tap per size/thread One thread mill can cut many sizes Material Suitability Risk of tap breakage in tough metals Better for hard-to-machine materials Thread Quality High-quality but fixed geometry Adjustable depth and excellent finish Chip Control Poor in blind holes Better evacuation and cleaner threads Cost Cheaper per tool Higher initial tool cost, lower long-term Thread Milling and Tapping in Different Materials When working with softer materials like aluminum or mild steel, tapping is fast and rarely problematic. But when dealing with: ● Stainless steel ● Tool steel ● Superalloys …thread milling provides better tool life and reduces the risk of tool breakage. This makes it a smart choice for aerospace, medical, and high-precision industries. CNC Programming Differences Tapping usually relies on a simple cycle (G84 for right-hand, G74 for left-hand tapping). Easy to program, minimal variables. Thread milling , on the other hand, requires: ● Circular interpolation (G02/G03) ● Depth control ● Helix angle programming While this adds complexity, modern CAM software and CNCs make it increasingly easier. Tool Life and Cost Considerations Taps wear out quickly in hard materials and can break, especially in blind holes with poor chip evacuation. Thread mills , although more expensive upfront, last longer and are more forgiving, especially if you’re threading near the bottom of a hole. Plus, if a thread mill breaks, you typically don’t lose the entire part. Is Thread Milling Better Than Tapping? It depends on your application. Tapping wins when: ● You're working in high-volume production ● Thread size and material are standard ● Speed and cost-per-hole are critical Thread milling is better when: ● You're threading expensive or difficult materials like Inconel or titanium ● You need flexibility in thread sizes or depths ● You want to avoid breaking taps in blind holes ● You're using CNC machines capable of helical interpolation So, is thread milling better than tapping ? In terms of flexibility and safety, yes. But in terms of speed and simplicity, tapping still holds the crown for everyday work. At JLCCNC , we specialize in precise, reliable threaded parts, no matter the size, material, or threading method. Whether you need help programming a thread milling cycle or want bulk tapping production , we’re here to help. Upload your design file and get a free quote here , we’ll recommend the best process for your job. Final Word: Which One Should You Use? Use tapping when: ● You need speed and low cost ● You’re working on large batches with consistent threads ● You have limited CNC capabilities Use thread milling when: ● You're working with tough or expensive materials ● Flexibility, precision, and thread quality matter ● You're threading blind holes or varying thread diameters Pro tip: If you’re threading critical parts, test both methods. A single broken tap can cost more than investing in a thread mill. Want More? Threading precision matters. Check out our guide on CNC tolerances and machining accuracy for a deeper understanding of how to control fit, finish, and dimensional repeatability. Whether you're working with tough materials, tight tolerances, or just want expert advice on choosing between thread milling and tapping , our CNC machining services have you covered. Published Jul 30, 2025, updated Jul 28, 2025 5 min Threading a hole sounds simple, until you’re deciding between thread milling and tapping . Both methods are staples in CNC machining and manual operations, but they serve different purposes, machines, and tolerances. Whether you're threading aluminum, stainless steel, or titanium, choosing the wrong method can mean broken tools, scrapped parts, or wasted hours. Let’s break down the real differences between thread milling vs tapping , when to use one over the other, and how to choose the right tool for your part. What is Tapping? Tapping is the traditional method of creating internal threads by driving a tap, a hardened cutting tool, into a pre-drilled hole. It’s fast, easy to set up, and widely used in manual and CNC operations. There are three common types of taps: ● Hand taps – used manually with a T-handle ● Spiral point taps – best for through holes ● Spiral flute taps – best for blind holes Taps are typically specific to one thread size and pitch, which makes them convenient but rigid in flexibility. What is Thread Milling? Thread milling , on the other hand, uses a rotating tool called a thread mill to cut threads with a helical interpolation motion. The tool enters the hole and follows a spiral path to form the thread, using a CNC program to control pitch and depth. There are three types of thread mills: ● Single-point thread mills – extremely flexible for custom threads ● Multi-form thread mills – cut the full profile in one pass ● Indexable thread mills – ideal for large threads or production runs Thread milling may require more programming and setup time, but it shines in areas tapping simply can't reach. Thread Milling vs Tapping: Head-to-Head Comparison Let’s stack up thread milling vs tapping in the areas that matter most: Feature Tapping Thread Milling Speed Faster for high-volume production Slower, especially for large threads Tool Flexibility One tap per size/thread One thread mill can cut many sizes Material Suitability Risk of tap breakage in tough metals Better for hard-to-machine materials Thread Quality High-quality but fixed geometry Adjustable depth and excellent finish Chip Control Poor in blind holes Better evacuation and cleaner threads Cost Cheaper per tool Higher initial tool cost, lower long-term Thread Milling and Tapping in Different Materials When working with softer materials like aluminum or mild steel, tapping is fast and rarely problematic. But when dealing with: ● Stainless steel ● Tool steel ● Superalloys …thread milling provides better tool life and reduces the risk of tool breakage. This makes it a smart choice for aerospace, medical, and high-precision industries. CNC Programming Differences Tapping usually relies on a simple cycle (G84 for right-hand, G74 for left-hand tapping). Easy to program, minimal variables. Thread milling , on the other hand, requires: ● Circular interpolation (G02/G03) ● Depth control ● Helix angle programming While this adds complexity, modern CAM software and CNCs make it increasingly easier. Tool Life and Cost Considerations Taps wear out quickly in hard materials and can break, especially in blind holes with poor chip evacuation. Thread mills , although more expensive upfront, last longer and are more forgiving, especially if you’re threading near the bottom of a hole. Plus, if a thread mill breaks, you typically don’t lose the entire part. Is Thread Milling Better Than Tapping? It depends on your application. Tapping wins when: ● You're working in high-volume production ● Thread size and material are standard ● Speed and cost-per-hole are critical Thread milling is better when: ● You're threading expensive or difficult materials like Inconel or titanium ● You need flexibility in thread sizes or depths ● You want to avoid breaking taps in blind holes ● You're using CNC machines capable of helical interpolation So, is thread milling better than tapping ? In terms of flexibility and safety, yes. But in terms of speed and simplicity, tapping still holds the crown for everyday work. Whether you need help programming a thread milling cycle or want bulk tapping production , we’re here to help. Upload your design file and get a free quote here , we’ll recommend the best process for your job. Final Word: Which One Should You Use? Use tapping when: ● You need speed and low cost ● You’re working on large batches with consistent threads ● You have limited CNC capabilities Use thread milling when: ● You're working with tough or expensive materials ● Flexibility, precision, and thread quality matter ● You're threading blind holes or varying thread diameters Pro tip: If you’re threading critical parts, test both methods. Published Jun 10, 2025, updated Jun 05, 2025 8 min Table of Contents Similarities Between Waterjet and Laser Cutting Waterjet vs Laser Cutting: Key Differences Cost Comparison: Which Sheet Metal Cutting Method Saves More? Speed and Precision: Which Sheet Metal Cutting Tool Performs Better? Materials & Thickness: What Can You Cut (and How Thick)? It’s a common question in fabrication, and one that sparks plenty of debate on shop floors and online forums alike: Waterjet or laser cutting? How to cut sheet metal in a way that gives you the cleanest cut, the best value, or the fastest turnaround? Here’s the thing: it’s not always a clear-cut answer. Both waterjet and laser cutting are precision powerhouses in the world of sheet metal fabrication. They each come with their own strengths, quirks, and best-use scenarios. Some projects demand the crisp accuracy of a laser, others the cold, abrasive power of high-pressure water, and sometimes, it’s a combination of both that gets the job done right. In this blog, we’re diving into the differences between waterjet and laser cutting , from how each method works to what materials they handle best, the cost and speed implications, and which process makes the most sense for your next job. If you’ve ever been torn between these two cutting technologies, we’re here to break it down, no fluff, just facts. Let’s get into it. Similarities Between Waterjet and Laser Cutting Before we dive into the differences, let’s clear one thing up: waterjet and laser cutting aren’t rivals as much as they are different tools in the same precision toolkit. In many ways, they share common ground, especially when it comes to their roles in modern sheet metal fabrication. Here are some key similarities: CNC Precision : Both processes rely on CNC (Computer Numerical Control) systems, meaning they’re incredibly accurate and highly repeatable. Once a CAD file is uploaded, both machines will follow it to the exact detail, cut after cut. No Physical Tooling Contact : Unlike traditional machining, neither method uses a physical cutting tool that touches the material. That means no tool wear , fewer mechanical stresses on the material, and a cleaner overall process. Versatility in Design : Both are ideal for cutting complex 2D profiles from sheet metal. Sharp corners, intricate curves, and tight inner contours? No problem for either. High Tolerances : Depending on the setup, both can achieve tolerances within a few thousandths of an inch. That level of precision makes them suitable for everything from aerospace components to high-end consumer products. Industry-Wide Applications : You’ll find waterjet and laser cutting used across a wide range of industries, automotive, aerospace, industrial design, signage, architecture, prototyping , and beyond. If it involves metal and demands clean, accurate cuts, chances are one of these methods is in play. Both waterjet and laser cutting are digitally controlled and offer excellent precision, making them powerful sheet metal cutting tools . Want to explore how laser compares to another popular digital method? Here's a detailed guide on the difference between CNC cutting and laser cutting. In short, both waterjet and laser cutting offer clean cuts, reliable repeatability, and flexible design possibilities . But once you start factoring in material type, thickness, budget, and speed, the differences really start to show. Speaking of which, let’s line them up side by side in a comparison table next. Waterjet vs Laser Cutting: Key Differences Feature/Factor Waterjet Cutting Laser Cutting Cutting Method High-pressure water + abrasive Focused laser beam Heat-Affected Zone (HAZ) None Present Ideal Materials Metals, stone, glass, composites Metals, some plastics, thin woods Max Thickness (Sheet Metal) Up to 6+ inches Typically under 1 inch (varies by metal) Tolerance/Precision ~±0.003" to ±0.005" ~±0.001" to ±0.003" Kerf Width Wider (~0.02" - 0.04") Narrower (~0.006" - 0.012") Cutting Speed Slower, especially on thick material Faster on thin-to-medium materials Surface Finish Matte/sanded edge Clean, slightly discolored edge Secondary Processing Often needed Often minimal Cost Comparison: Which Sheet Metal Cutting Method Saves More? (source: Freepik) When it comes to sheet metal cutting , cost is often the deciding factor, especially for production runs or budget-sensitive projects. While both waterjet cutting and laser cutting of metal sheets offer precision and versatility, the overall expense of each method can vary widely depending on a few key factors. Let’s break it down: 1. Equipment and Operation Costs Laser cutting machines tend to have a higher upfront investment. However, they’re generally faster and more energy-efficient , which can reduce per-part costs over time, especially for thinner materials. Waterjet cutting systems , on the other hand, come with lower thermal risk but higher ongoing costs due to the use of abrasive materials , pumps, and higher maintenance needs. 2. Consumables and Power Use Laser cutters primarily use gas (like nitrogen or oxygen) and electricity. These costs scale with power and material thickness, but there’s no abrasive to replace. Waterjets consume a lot of water and require a constant supply of garnet abrasive. Over time, abrasive costs can add up significantly , especially for long or thick cuts. 3. Maintenance and Downtime Waterjet systems have more moving parts and higher wear-and-tear from the abrasive flow. Expect more downtime for maintenance and consumable replacement. Laser cutters require less mechanical upkeep, which means more uptime and faster production cycles , particularly for thin cut sheet metal jobs. 4. Material Waste and Post-Processing Laser cutting sheet metal usually produces cleaner edges with minimal kerf, which means less post-processing and lower finishing costs. Waterjet cutting might leave a rougher edge or more taper, especially on thick stock, which could require additional machining. 5. Real-World Cost Examples For thin-gauge materials like aluminum or stainless steel (under 1/4"), laser cutting is typically the most cost-effective way to cut sheet metal , faster, cleaner, and more economical per part. For thick or exotic materials (like titanium, stone, or composites), waterjet cutting may be more cost-effective despite slower speeds, since it doesn’t risk warping the material or requiring costly rework. Speed and Precision: Which Sheet Metal Cutting Tool Performs Better? (source: Pexels) In sheet metal fabrication, speed and precision aren’t just nice-to-haves, they’re make-or-break factors. Whether you’re cranking out hundreds of parts or creating a one-off prototype, the right sheet metal cutting tool can dramatically impact turnaround time and final quality. Let’s see how sheet meta l laser cutting and waterjet cutting stack up when it comes to cutting speed and edge precision. Speed: Laser Wins the Race (Most of the Time) Laser cutting is incredibly quick, particularly when working with thin to medium-thickness metal sheets. The focused laser beam can slice through materials like stainless steel or aluminum with incredible efficiency. If you're cutting a run of 0.125" stainless brackets, for example, laser cutting sheet metal might finish the entire job in minutes. Compare that to waterjet cutting, while it’s powerful, it’s not known for speed . The process is slower because it mechanically erodes the material rather than vaporizing it. A 0.5" thick aluminum plate might take a waterjet several minutes to cut through, whereas a laser would be done in a fraction of the time, assuming the thickness is within the laser's optimal range. Example: Cutting a batch of 1/8" mild steel electrical enclosures? Go with laser cutting for quicker production. Cutting a custom piece from 2" thick steel? Waterjet’s your best bet. Precision: Depends on the Material and Thickness Both methods are highly accurate , but they shine under different conditions. Laser cutting delivers ultra-fine detail and tighter tolerances, often as precise as ±0.001", especially on thinner materials. This makes it ideal for projects requiring tight fitment, intricate geometries , or minimal post-processing. Waterjet cutting is also accurate, generally around ±0.003" to ±0.005", but it can suffer from tapering on thick materials if not properly controlled. However, it has a great advantage: no heat-affected zone (HAZ) . That means zero risk of material warping, which can preserve mechanical properties in heat-sensitive metals. Example: Need finely detailed stainless steel signage with sharp internal cutouts? Laser cutting is the answer. Cutting heat-treated tool steel or titanium that can’t afford any heat distortion? Waterjet wins. Edge Quality: Smooth vs. Matte Laser cutting leaves a smooth, often shiny edge, great for visible parts or components going straight to assembly. Waterjet typically leaves a matte, sandblasted edge. It's clean, but may require extra finishing if aesthetics matter. Materials & Thickness: What Can You Cut (and How Thick)? (source: Unsplash) When it comes to how to cut sheet metal , your material choice and thickness often make the decision for you. Laser cutting excels with thin to moderately thick metal sheets<dynamic-value> aluminum, stainless, and mild steel up to around 0.75". It struggles with highly reflective materials (like copper) and anything too thick, which can reduce cut quality or slow production significantly. Waterjet cutting , on the other hand, can slice through virtually anything: metals, composites, stone, even glass , and up to 6 inches thick or more . No melting, no HAZ, and no material limitations. Quick takeaway: If you're working with thick or exotic materials, waterjet is your go-to. For fast, clean cuts on standard gauge metal, laser cutting is typically more efficient. That level of precision makes them suitable for everything from aerospace components to high-end consumer products. Industry-Wide Applications : You’ll find waterjet and laser cutting used across a wide range of industries, automotive, aerospace, industrial design, signage, architecture, prototyping , and beyond. If it involves metal and demands clean, accurate cuts, chances are one of these methods is in play. Both waterjet and laser cutting are digitally controlled and offer excellent precision, making them powerful sheet metal cutting tools . Want to explore how laser compares to another popular digital method? Here's a detailed guide on the difference between CNC cutting and laser cutting. In short, both waterjet and laser cutting offer clean cuts, reliable repeatability, and flexible design possibilities . But once you start factoring in material type, thickness, budget, and speed, the differences really start to show. Speaking of which, let’s line them up side by side in a comparison table next. Waterjet vs Laser Cutting: Key Differences Feature/Factor Waterjet Cutting Laser Cutting Cutting Method High-pressure water + abrasive Focused laser beam Heat-Affected Zone (HAZ) None Present Ideal Materials Metals, stone, glass, composites Metals, some plastics, thin woods Max Thickness (Sheet Metal) Up to 6+ inches Typically under 1 inch (varies by metal) Tolerance/Precision ~±0.003" to ±0.005" ~±0.001" to ±0.003" Kerf Width Wider (~0.02" - 0.04") Narrower (~0.006" - 0.012") Cutting Speed Slower, especially on thick material Faster on thin-to-medium materials Surface Finish Matte/sanded edge Clean, slightly discolored edge Secondary Processing Often needed Often minimal Cost Comparison: Which Sheet Metal Cutting Method Saves More? (source: Freepik) When it comes to sheet metal cutting , cost is often the deciding factor, especially for production runs or budget-sensitive projects. While both waterjet cutting and laser cutting of metal sheets offer precision and versatility, the overall expense of each method can vary widely depending on a few key factors. Let’s break it down: 1. Equipment and Operation Costs Laser cutting machines tend to have a higher upfront investment. However, they’re generally faster and more energy-efficient , which can reduce per-part costs over time, especially for thinner materials. Waterjet cutting systems , on the other hand, come with lower thermal risk but higher ongoing costs due to the use of abrasive materials , pumps, and higher maintenance needs. 2. Consumables and Power Use Laser cutters primarily use gas (like nitrogen or oxygen) and electricity. These costs scale with power and material thickness, but there’s no abrasive to replace. Waterjets consume a lot of water and require a constant supply of garnet abrasive. Over time, abrasive costs can add up significantly , especially for long or thick cuts. 3. Maintenance and Downtime Waterjet systems have more moving parts and higher wear-and-tear from the abrasive flow. Expect more downtime for maintenance and consumable replacement. Laser cutters require less mechanical upkeep, which means more uptime and faster production cycles , particularly for thin cut sheet metal jobs. 4. Material Waste and Post-Processing Laser cutting sheet metal usually produces cleaner edges with minimal kerf, which means less post-processing and lower finishing costs. Waterjet cutting might leave a rougher edge or more taper, especially on thick stock, which could require additional machining. 5. Real-World Cost Examples For thin-gauge materials like aluminum or stainless steel (under 1/4"), laser cutting is typically the most cost-effective way to cut sheet metal , faster, cleaner, and more economical per part. For thick or exotic materials (like titanium, stone, or composites), waterjet cutting may be more cost-effective despite slower speeds, since it doesn’t risk warping the material or requiring costly rework. Speed and Precision: Which Sheet Metal Cutting Tool Performs Better? (source: Pexels) In sheet metal fabrication, speed and precision aren’t just nice-to-haves, they’re make-or-break factors. Whether you’re cranking out hundreds of parts or creating a one-off prototype, the right sheet metal cutting tool can dramatically impact turnaround time and final quality. Let’s see how sheet meta l laser cutting and waterjet cutting stack up when it comes to cutting speed and edge precision. Speed: Laser Wins the Race (Most of the Time) Laser cutting is incredibly quick, particularly when working with thin to medium-thickness metal sheets. The focused laser beam can slice through materials like stainless steel or aluminum with incredible efficiency. If you're cutting a run of 0.125" stainless brackets, for example, laser cutting sheet metal might finish the entire job in minutes. Compare that to waterjet cutting, while it’s powerful, it’s not known for speed . The process is slower because it mechanically erodes the material rather than vaporizing it. A 0.5" thick aluminum plate might take a waterjet several minutes to cut through, whereas a laser would be done in a fraction of the time, assuming the thickness is within the laser's optimal range. Example: Cutting a batch of 1/8" mild steel electrical enclosures? Go with laser cutting for quicker production. Cutting a custom piece from 2" thick steel? Waterjet’s your best bet. Precision: Depends on the Material and Thickness Both methods are highly accurate , but they shine under different conditions. Laser cutting delivers ultra-fine detail and tighter tolerances, often as precise as ±0.001", especially on thinner materials. This makes it ideal for projects requiring tight fitment, intricate geometries , or minimal post-processing. Waterjet cutting is also accurate, generally around ±0.003" to ±0.005", but it can suffer from tapering on thick materials if not properly controlled. However, it has a great advantage: no heat-affected zone (HAZ) . That means zero risk of material warping, which can preserve mechanical properties in heat-sensitive metals. Example: Need finely detailed stainless steel signage with sharp internal cutouts? Laser cutting is the answer. Cutting heat-treated tool steel or titanium that can’t afford any heat distortion? Waterjet wins. Edge Quality: Smooth vs. Matte Laser cutting leaves a smooth, often shiny edge, great for visible parts or components going straight to assembly. Waterjet typically leaves a matte, sandblasted edge. It's clean, but may require extra finishing if aesthetics matter. Materials & Thickness: What Can You Cut (and How Thick)? (source: Unsplash) When it comes to how to cut sheet metal , your material choice and thickness often make the decision for you. Laser cutting excels with thin to moderately thick metal sheets<dynamic-value> aluminum, stainless, and mild steel up to around 0.75". It struggles with highly reflective materials (like copper) and anything too thick, which can reduce cut quality or slow production significantly. Waterjet cutting , on the other hand, can slice through virtually anything: metals, composites, stone, even glass , and up to 6 inches thick or more . No melting, no HAZ, and no material limitations. Quick takeaway: If you're working with thick or exotic materials, waterjet is your go-to. For fast, clean cuts on standard gauge metal, laser cutting is typically more efficient. Types of Holes in CNC Machining Blind Hole Machining Explained Blind Hole Tapping (Blind Hole Tap) Designing Blind Holes for CNC Manufacturing FAQ What Is a Blind Hole? Types of Holes and CNC Hole Machining Explained In CNC machining, few operations challenge process control and tool stability as much as blind hole machining. A blind hole is a hole that terminates at a defined internal depth rather than breaking through the opposite surface. Because the cavity is enclosed at the bottom, chip evacuation, thermal behavior, tool wear, and dimensional accuracy become far more difficult to manage compared to through-hole machining. These constraints make blind holes indispensable yet technically demanding features across precision mechanical parts, sealed housings, consumer products, and structural components. When projects require consistently accurate blind hole drilling, tapping, or fine-tolerance cavity machining, J LCCNC provides reliable depth control , specialized tool paths, and clean internal finishes, supporting both prototypes and full production. What Is a Blind Hole? (Quora) A blind hole is defined by its closed end. Unlike a through hole, which passes entirely through a workpiece, a blind hole stops before reaching the opposite side. The bottom shape varies depending on the tool used: conventional drills produce conical bottoms, whereas flat-bottom drills and end mills generate planar surfaces suitable for precision assemblies or tapping. The engineering purpose of blind holes extends well beyond simply preventing penetration. In structural parts, maintaining a continuous opposite surface preserves rigidity, prevents stress risers, and helps sustain load paths. In pressurized or sealed systems—pneumatic housings, pump bodies, battery enclosures—blind holes prevent leakage of fluids or gases. In aesthetic or ergonomic products, they allow components to be fastened internally without exposing screw holes on the exterior. Blind holes essentially balance internal functionality with external appearance, mechanical strength, and environmental protection. Blind Hole vs Through Hole Through holes are straightforward to machine because chips naturally exit, tools experience less thermal stress, and depth accuracy is less sensitive. Blind holes demand precise programming—typically down to fractions of a millimeter—because any error may result in breakthrough. Through holes favor higher cutting speeds and simpler setups, whereas blind holes influence manufacturing costs due to slower feeds, peck cycles, coolant optimization, and bottom-clearance requirements. This difference in machining complexity explains why blind hole features often drive DFM (Design for Manufacturability) considerations. Types of Holes in CNC Machining Hole geometry in CNC machining reflects functional intent. Through holes support fasteners, shafts, dowel pins, and alignment features, making them ideal for high-speed fabrication. Countersunk holes allow screws to sit flush with the surface, maintaining flatness in precision mechanical surfaces. Counterbores accommodate socket-cap screws and create controlled seating planes for load-bearing joints. Within this landscape, blind holes occupy a specialized category. They enable internal threads, hidden fastening points, or mounting cavities that must not disturb the profile or sealing plane of the component. In industrial machinery, blind holes allow assembly without compromising fluid channels or structural ribs. In consumer electronics, they maintain the clean, uninterrupted outer surfaces expected from modern design. The choice between blind and through holes ultimately depends on the balance between manufacturability and functional necessity. Blind Hole Machining Explained (Science Direct) Blind hole machining is more complex than ordinary drilling because the tool must operate inside a confined cavity with no path for chips to escape. As the flutes fill with chips, heat rises sharply and causes accelerated tool wear or material hardening, especially in stainless steel and titanium. This is why blind hole drilling strategies emphasize controlled chip load, coolant access, and stable tool geometry. Drilling Blind Holes Standard twist drills are used for most metals, but they form a conical bottom that may not meet design requirements. When engineers need a flat-bottomed blind hole—for example, to optimize the thread engagement length or to improve seating conditions—a flat-bottom drill or end mill is applied. Peck drilling cycles become essential in deeper holes, where periodic retraction clears chips and reduces heat. In high-precision applications, depth is repeatedly verified using machine probing or tool setters to ensure no risk of breakthrough. Depth Control and Tool Selection Depth accuracy is one of the defining challenges in blind hole machining. CNC tools rely on tool length offsets, spindle probing, or laser measurement systems to maintain consistency. Carbide drills offer superior rigidity for deeper holes, while coatings such as TiAlN or AlTiN stabilize cutting edges under heat. The selected tool often reflects not only the material but also the hole’s final function—threaded, reamed, or used as a locating feature. Material Behavior in Blind Hole Drilling Aluminum machines easily but forms long, continuous chips that can clog a blind cavity unless chip-breaking geometries are used. Stainless steel hardens quickly under heat and demands strict lubrication control. Titanium concentrates heat at the cutting edge, often requiring through-tool coolant systems. Engineering plastics behave differently—they may melt or smear if spindle speeds are excessive. The interaction between tool, material, and confined cavity defines the entire machining strategy for blind holes. Blind Hole Tapping (Blind Hole Tap) (Science Direct) Blind hole tapping is one of the most technically sensitive procedures in CNC machining. Unlike through-hole tapping, where excess chips simply exit the opposite side, blind hole tapping traps chips at the bottom. If unmanaged, these chips compact and cause tap breakage. Bottoming Taps for Blind Holes A blind hole tap—usually a bottoming tap—features very little chamfer, enabling threads to form almost to the bottom of the cavity. This is crucial when the full thread depth is needed for load-bearing joints, especially in aerospace or automotive parts. Plug taps and taper taps have longer chamfers and are not suitable for holes where thread engagement must begin close to the bottom. Best Practices for Tapping Blind Holes Effective blind hole tapping relies on rigid tapping cycles, stable lubrication, and precise pilot hole sizing. In difficult materials, spiral-flute taps help extract chips upward, preventing compaction at the bottom of the hole. Thread milling is often chosen when the material is prone to chip welding or when the design requires extremely tight tolerance control. The entire process must anticipate torque spikes, potential chip packing, and sensitivity to tool wear. Designing Blind Holes for CNC Manufacturing Blind hole design affects machinability more than most engineers initially assume. Hole depth must align with available drill and tap geometries, ensuring that tools do not deflect excessively. The bottom clearance should reflect the type of threading operation planned, and thin walls around the hole must be avoided to prevent distortion during machining. Depth, Diameter, and Tolerance The ratio between hole depth and diameter heavily influences tool stability. Excessively deep blind holes increase the likelihood of tool vibration, poor chip evacuation, and dimensional variation. Tolerance selection must reflect not only fit and function but also the realities of machining inside a confined space. Surface finish is another consideration: smoother walls reduce thread friction, improve fastener performance, and reduce wear during repeated assembly cycles. FAQ What is the purpose of a blind hole? To enable internal mounting, threading, or functional cavities without penetrating the opposite surface, preserving structure, sealing integrity, or aesthetics. Why is blind hole machining more complex than through holes? Restricted chip flow, higher heat concentration, and tighter depth accuracy requirements. How are blind holes tapped successfully? With bottoming taps, rigid cycles, proper lubrication, and chip evacuation strategies such as spiral flutes or thread milling. What is blind hole drilling? A controlled-depth drilling process designed to terminate precisely before breakthrough. Tolerance selection must reflect not only fit and function but also the realities of machining inside a confined space. Why is blind hole machining more complex than through holes? Restricted chip flow, higher heat concentration, and tighter depth accuracy requirements. How are blind holes tapped successfully? With bottoming taps, rigid cycles, proper lubrication, and chip evacuation strategies such as spiral flutes or thread milling. What is blind hole drilling? A controlled-depth drilling process designed to terminate precisely before breakthrough.
