Unlock Color PCB Printing with PCBWay! by: PCBWay Mar 08,2024 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in News Color PCB Printing PCBWay Service Nowadays, traditional PCB printing technology can no longer meet the aesthetic requirements of modern circuit board production. To better fulfill customers' design needs, we are pleased to announce that PCBWay has introduced UV printing equipment. This equipment utilizes UV-curable inks to achieve high-quality image printing on various materials, including fiberglass boards, metal substrates, ceramic substrates, flexible boards, and rigid-flex boards. Entrance https://www.pcbway.com/orderonline.aspx Prerequisites for Ordering Maximum size for a single piece: 270*470MM; Selection of background soldermask color required. Design Specifications Drill holes, traces, soldermasks, and outline designs must comply with specifications. Avoid placing colored characters in areas with solder mask openings, such as surface-mount pads or through-hole pads. What kind of files should be provided for color printing? Method One : Draw colored characters on the silkscreen layer of the Gerber and provide reference pictures. For example: Method Two : If you include information about colored silkscreen in the Gerber layer, each individual color must have its own layer. If there is only one layer, we can only print one color. [This method is not recommended] . If you need to print in multiple colors, we recommend using method One and providing us with a reference picture. 4.Please send the images you want to print on the PCB in the following formats: AI, PDF, JPEG, PNG, TIFF, etc., and indicate your desired printing location on the board. 5.If the image contains a QR code, please ensure that the QR code can be accurately scanned and recognized. Note : If you choose UV printing Multi-color, we will use matte UV color printing by default. When designing the colored characters on the bottom layer, be careful not to design the colored characters as mirrored inverses. (The process of color printing is different from that of standard PCB silkscreen printing. When printing colorful characters on the bottom layer, they are printed with the bottom layer of the PCB facing up.) For situations where the entire top or bottom side requires full-color printing, regardless of the solder mask color you choose, we will use a white solder mask on the full-color printed side and then proceed with the color printing. This is for a better printing effect. Please upload the print image, positioning image, and Gerber in one compressed file. By providing a clear positioning image and necessary instructions, you can assist PCBWay in accurately determining and achieving the desired printing position. Matte UV Color Printing vs. Glossy UV Color Printing Matte ink does not increase the overall thickness, and the PCB's appearance looks smooth. Glossy ink increases the overall thickness and may affect the soldering of component pads. The appearance is beautiful but uneven. Features Adopting UV-LED lamp curing, which enables instant drying, can significantly enhances production efficiency. UV printing technology employs UV-curable inks, ensuring firm and clear printing information resistant to fading, thus enhancing product identification and aesthetics. The normal print survives SMT reflow. UV printing technology can present images in various colors and styles, meeting customers' personalized requirements. Professional industrial-grade UV printers support high-precision printing, delivering exquisite results whether on flat panels or rolled materials. Unlike traditional printing methods, UV printing does not produce volatile organic compounds during the production process, ensuring air quality in the production workshop and providing employees with a safer and healthier working environment. FAQ on UV Printing: Can the UV printed surface be cleaned with water? Yes, it can be cleaned with water. Can the UV printed surface be cleaned with alcohol? It is more difficult to clean after being exposed to alcohol and baked (currently, the board undergoes a short baking process after UV printing). However, with increased contact time with alcohol and vigorous scrubbing, it can be removed. This also depends on whether the UV is on the copper surface or the solder mask surface. How hard is the UV printed surface (sensitivity to scratches)? The UV surface is not sensitive to scratches. However, compared to the solder mask, it is less scratch-resistant because UV printing is ink that is sprayed on and is relatively thin. Welcome to give it a try if you're interested! Besides, PCBWay will continue to enhance its manufacturing capabilities to bring more choices and personalized services to customers in the future. Verify Now Blog > 0402 vs 0603 Capacitor for High-Speed PCB Decoupling 0402 vs 0603 Capacitor for High-Speed PCB Decoupling by: Mila Sep 16,2026 <dynamic-value> <dynamic-value> Posted in PCB Design & Layout decoupling capacitor 0402 capacitor 0603 capacitor 0402 vs 0603 capacitor A common misconception is that a larger capacitor package stores more energy and therefore provides better filtering performance. However, in high-speed PCB designs such as FPGA, SoC, and DDR applications, 0402 capacitors with a typical value of 0.1 μF are commonly placed near BGA core power pins instead of larger 0603 capacitors. For the same nominal capacitance, the key difference in 0402 vs 0603 capacitor performance is not how much charge the capacitor stores, but its equivalent series inductance (ESL). At lower frequencies, the performance difference between package sizes is usually less significant. As the operating frequency enters the MHz range and above, ESL increasingly affects the impedance and effective frequency range of a decoupling capacitor. The Underlying Principle: Equivalent Series Inductance (ESL) A surface-mount capacitor is not an ideal capacitor. Its equivalent circuit typically consists of an ideal capacitance (C), equivalent series resistance (ESR), and equivalent series inductance (ESL). ESL comes from the entire current path, including the internal electrodes, terminations, PCB pads, traces, and power/ground vias. Inductance opposes rapidly changing current, and its effect becomes more significant as frequency increases. Every capacitor has a self-resonant frequency (SRF): Operating frequency < SRF: The device behaves mainly as a capacitor and can perform its decoupling function normally. Operating frequency > SRF: The device gradually becomes inductive, and its high-frequency decoupling capability decreases. A higher self-resonant frequency generally means that a decoupling capacitor can maintain low impedance over a wider high-frequency range. For example, consider 0402 and 0603 capacitors with the same nominal capacitance of 0.1 μF: 0603 capacitor: Its larger body size generally results in a longer internal current path and higher intrinsic parasitic inductance. 0402 capacitor: Its smaller body size generally provides a shorter current path and lower intrinsic parasitic inductance. Therefore, under similar capacitance and component structures, a 0402 capacitor typically has lower parasitic inductance and a higher self-resonant frequency than a 0603 capacitor, making it more suitable for high-frequency decoupling. The actual ESL and SRF values should be verified from the component datasheet or the manufacturer's high-frequency model. PCB Pads and Vias Also Add Parasitic Inductance Engineers often focus only on the capacitor's intrinsic ESL specified in the datasheet. However, in a complete power delivery network, PCB pads, traces, and vias also introduce parasitic inductance and can sometimes have an even greater impact than the capacitor itself. In an 0402 vs 0603 capacitor comparison, the larger pads and spacing of a 0603 package can make the connection between the capacitor and power/ground vias longer. This additional trace length increases the total loop inductance. The smaller pads of a 0402 capacitor make it easier to place power and ground vias close to the component. When the PCB manufacturing and assembly processes allow it, microvias or Via-in-Pad can also be used to further shorten the current path and reduce the power-to-ground loop area. When an IC core suddenly draws high-frequency transient current, the total inductance of the current loop affects the power response. Even a capacitor with excellent electrical characteristics may provide limited high-frequency decoupling if the current path is too long. This is why the key advantage of a 0402 capacitor is not simply its smaller package size, but its ability to help create a smaller and lower-inductance current loop. （Optimized Layout） 0402 vs 0603 Capacitor: Advantages and Limitations Advantages of 0402 Capacitors Lower intrinsic parasitic inductance and typically higher SRF, providing better performance for high-frequency decoupling; Smaller pads allow the capacitor to be placed closer to BGA power pins and return paths, reducing the power-to-ground loop area; Higher placement density allows more decoupling capacitors to be placed around BGA devices, helping optimize PDN impedance; The smaller package makes it easier to implement compact power and ground via arrangements and, when supported by the PCB process, microvia or Via-in-Pad structures. Limitations of 0402 Capacitors In the same component series, the available capacitance and voltage-rating options may be more limited, while the actual effective capacitance can also decrease under DC bias; For the same capacitance and voltage rating, the component cost may be higher than that of a 0603 capacitor; Manual soldering is more difficult, with a higher risk of insufficient soldering or component loss, and mass production requires tighter stencil and placement process control; At relatively low frequencies, the performance difference between 0402 and 0603 is usually small, so a 0402 capacitor does not need to be selected simply because it is smaller. When to Use 0603 Capacitors They can generally provide sufficient performance in lower-frequency filtering applications; The larger package can make it easier to obtain suitable capacitance, voltage ratings, and mechanical reliability; They are easier to solder manually and can be suitable for general power filtering and decoupling applications where high-frequency performance is not the primary concern. Therefore, the choice between an 0402 vs 0603 capacitor should not be based on a fixed frequency boundary. As frequency increases, the ESL differences introduced by the component package and PCB mounting structure become increasingly important. The actual selection should consider effective capacitance, ESR, ESL, SRF, and the PCB layout together. Key Considerations for Decoupling Capacitor Selection and Layout Place decoupling capacitors as close as possible to BGA core power pins and other power pins that require high-frequency transient current. A 0402 capacitor is often preferred for these applications. The goal is to reduce the total parasitic inductance of the current loop and improve high-frequency PDN impedance. For DC-DC outputs and other applications where mounting inductance is less critical, 0603 or even 0805 packages can be selected according to effective capacitance, voltage rating, cost, and manufacturing requirements. Loop area is more important than package size alone. This is a common misconception in PCB decoupling. A 0402 capacitor placed far away from the IC power and return path may provide poorer high-frequency performance than a 0603 capacitor placed directly along the current path. Package size is only one factor affecting parasitic inductance. The total power-to-ground loop inductance is more important. Component placement, pad design, and via location all play an important role in PCB decoupling. Do not blindly move to a 0201 package. As the package becomes smaller, the reduction in ESL can provide diminishing returns because the PCB mounting structure can become a larger part of the total inductance. At the same time, soldering difficulty, placement requirements, and component costs may increase. A 0402 capacitor is therefore a common balance between performance, board space, and manufacturing cost in many high-speed PDN designs, although the final package should always be selected according to the specific device and manufacturing process. Common Misconceptions About Decoupling Capacitors ❌ Misconception 1: A larger capacitor package stores more energy and therefore provides better decoupling. ✅ Reality: Under the same effective capacitance and operating conditions, package size itself does not determine how much energy a capacitor stores. The high-frequency performance difference between an 0402 capacitor and a 0603 capacitor mainly comes from parasitic parameters associated with the capacitor and its PCB mounting structure, with ESL being an important factor. ❌ Misconception 2: If the capacitance is the same, the package does not matter. ✅ Reality: Even with the same nominal capacitance, different packages can have different ESL, ESR, and SRF characteristics. During decoupling capacitor selection and PDN impedance simulation, models that match the actual component and PCB mounting structure should be used whenever possible. Otherwise, the simulated impedance curve and resonance characteristics may differ significantly from the actual result. For high-speed PCB decoupling, component selection should therefore go beyond nominal capacitance. The package, effective capacitance, ESL, SRF, and—most importantly—the complete current-loop PCB layout should all be considered. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. A 0402 capacitor is often preferred for these applications. The goal is to reduce the total parasitic inductance of the current loop and improve high-frequency PDN impedance. For DC-DC outputs and other applications where mounting inductance is less critical, 0603 or even 0805 packages can be selected according to effective capacitance, voltage rating, cost, and manufacturing requirements. Loop area is more important than package size alone. This is a common misconception in PCB decoupling. A 0402 capacitor placed far away from the IC power and return path may provide poorer high-frequency performance than a 0603 capacitor placed directly along the current path. Package size is only one factor affecting parasitic inductance. The total power-to-ground loop inductance is more important. Component placement, pad design, and via location all play an important role in PCB decoupling. Do not blindly move to a 0201 package. As the package becomes smaller, the reduction in ESL can provide diminishing returns because the PCB mounting structure can become a larger part of the total inductance. At the same time, soldering difficulty, placement requirements, and component costs may increase. A 0402 capacitor is therefore a common balance between performance, board space, and manufacturing cost in many high-speed PDN designs, although the final package should always be selected according to the specific device and manufacturing process. Common Misconceptions About Decoupling Capacitors ❌ Misconception 1: A larger capacitor package stores more energy and therefore provides better decoupling. ✅ Reality: Under the same effective capacitance and operating conditions, package size itself does not determine how much energy a capacitor stores. The high-frequency performance difference between an 0402 capacitor and a 0603 capacitor mainly comes from parasitic parameters associated with the capacitor and its PCB mounting structure, with ESL being an important factor. ❌ Misconception 2: If the capacitance is the same, the package does not matter. ✅ Reality: Even with the same nominal capacitance, different packages can have different ESL, ESR, and SRF characteristics. During decoupling capacitor selection and PDN impedance simulation, models that match the actual component and PCB mounting structure should be used whenever possible. Otherwise, the simulated impedance curve and resonance characteristics may differ significantly from the actual result. For high-speed PCB decoupling, component selection should therefore go beyond nominal capacitance. The package, effective capacitance, ESL, SRF, and—most importantly—the complete current-loop PCB layout should all be considered. Enter the year of your birth and check your Chinese Zodiac. AtomS3R AI Chatbot Kit 0402 vs 0603 Capacitor for High-Speed PCB Decoupling Turning Student Ideas into Real Projects with the PCBWay Future Innovators Program Talking about the Composition of PCB Price Over the years, PCB price changes have been familiar with people inside and outside the industry, even though some people with years of experience in the PCB industry may not fully understand the ins and outs of this, so to analyze the main factors affecting pcb price: The diversity of prices caused by the different materials used in PCBs is based on common double-sided boards. Sheets generally include fr-4, cem-3, etc., and board thickness varies from 0.2mm to 5.0mm, and copper thickness varies from 0.5oz to 3oz. All of these have resulted in huge price differences on the sheet material; in solder mask inks, there are also certain price differences between ordinary thermoset oils and photosensitive green oils, and thus the diversity of materials has caused price diversity. The different production processes used by PCBs result in different production processes with different prices that will result in different costs. Such as gold-plated plates and sprayed tin plates, the production of the shape of the milling (milling) plate and beer (red) plate, the use of silk screen lines and dry film lines will have different costs, resulting in a variety of prices. The diversity of prices caused by the difficulty of the PCB itself Even if the material is the same, the process is the same, but the difficulty of the PCB itself will result in different costs. For example, if there are 1000 holes on both boards, the hole diameter of one board is more than 0.6mm and the hole diameter of the other board is less than 0.6mm, different drilling costs will be formed; if the two boards are the same, the linewidth is different. Differently, one type is larger than 0.2mm and one type is smaller than 0.2mm, which also causes different production costs, because the scrap rate of difficult plates is high, the inevitable cost is increased, and the price diversity is thus caused. Different customer requirements will also cause different prices The level of customer demand will directly affect the plate production rate, such as a board by ipc-a-600e, class1 requirements have a 98% pass rate, but according to class3 requirements may be only 90% The passing rate, resulting in different costs for the mill, eventually led to a change in the price of the product. The diversity of prices caused by different PCB manufacturers even if the same product, but because of different manufacturers of technology and equipment, different levels of technology, will also form a different cost, nowadays many manufacturers like to produce tin spray plate, because the process is simple, low cost, but Some manufacturers also produce gold-plated plates, resulting in higher scrap rates and higher costs. Therefore, they prefer to produce tin-spray plates, so their prices for tin-spray plates are lower than those for gold-plated plates. The price difference caused by different payment methods At present, PCB manufacturers generally adjust PCB prices according to different payment methods, ranging from 5% to 10%, which also results in price differences. Diversification of prices caused by regional differences At present, from the geographical point of view, prices have been increasing from south to north. There are certain differences in prices in different regions, and thus different regions have also caused price diversity. events.before: Resources / Machining Design / Reaming: How It Works, Applications, Advantages, and Disadvantages Reaming: How It Works, Applications, Advantages, and Disadvantages Written by Dean McClements 11 min read Published May 30, 2024 Updated August 17, 2026 Reaming is a precision machining operation used to enhance the diameter and finish of a pre-drilled hole. It involves a multi-edged tool known as a reamer, which meticulously carves out material to achieve a highly accurate hole size and smooth surface finish. This process is important in industries in which exact dimensions and finishes are imperative, such as: aerospace, automotive, and medical device manufacturing. One benefit of reaming is that it can create uniform, high-quality holes with little tool wear and at a comparatively low cost. Nevertheless, it also has drawbacks<dynamic-value> the need for pre-machined holes and the risk of tool damage when not used properly. This article will discuss reaming, its procedure, the types and designs of reamers, and their vital function in contemporary production. What Is Reaming in Manufacturing? In manufacturing, reaming is a finishing operation that precisely enlarges and smooths the diameter of a pre-drilled hole. It is performed using a multi-edged tool called a reamer, which removes a small amount of material to improve the dimensional accuracy and surface finish of the hole. This process ensures that the holes meet strict specifications for size and finish, which is essential in high-precision engineering applications. Reaming is distinguished from other hole-finishing processes by its ability to achieve tight tolerances and a high-quality surface finish. What Is the Purpose of Reaming in Manufacturing? In the production process, reaming helps to precisely finish drilled holes, so they have a smooth surface and exact dimensions. It makes it possible to produce more holes of consistently good quality. When a precise, even surface is required, the technique is essential and calls for an appropriate edge profile and diameter. What Is the Other Term for Reaming? While "reaming" is the most commonly used term, it can also be referred to as "reamer machining" when discussing the process in a manufacturing context. This term emphasizes the use of the reamer tool in the machining operation. How Does Reaming Work? Reaming works by using a multi-edged rotary cutting tool called a reamer to enlarge and finish the surface of pre-drilled holes. The reamer's edges scrape away a thin layer of material, improving the hole's diameter accuracy and surface finish. It's a critical step for achieving tight tolerances and a high-quality surface in precision-engineering applications. How Does Reaming Differ From Drilling? Reaming differs from drilling in that it is a finishing process used to refine the size and improve the surface finish of an existing hole, rather than creating a new hole. Drilling is the initial process of cutting a circular-shaped hole in a workpiece, while reaming uses a reamer to smooth and accurately size the hole created by drilling. Reaming removes significantly less material than drilling and is focused on precision rather than hole creation. What Are the Applications of Reaming? Reaming’s ability to create precise holes with excellent surface finishes makes it widely employed in a variety of sectors. Here are some examples of reaming's uses in various industries: 1. Medical In orthopedic surgery, reaming is a vital process for preparing bones for intramedullary nailing, crucial in repairing long bone fractures. It also plays a significant role in joint-replacement procedures, in which accurate hole dimensions are paramount for the proper fitting and function of joint implants. This precision ensures the longevity and success of surgical outcomes, making reaming indispensable in medical device fabrication. 2. Manufacturing Reaming is an essential last step in the manufacturing industry that smoothes holes in precision products, such as tools and equipment parts. Achieving the precise tolerances and flawless surface finishes required for high-precision products' functionality and quality is largely dependent on this technique. It ensures that components fit together perfectly, improving the manufactured goods' overall integrity and functionality. 3. Automotive In the automotive sector, reaming plays a pivotal role in precision tasks such as enlarging and perfecting holes in vital engine components. This process guarantees that parts like brake systems and suspension units meet exact size specifications and possess a refined finish, essential for optimal vehicle performance and safety. 4. Pumps One procedure that is essential to the manufacturing of pumps is reaming. It's important to ensure that parts like impellers and casings have the precise size of holes needed for optimum performance. This precision ensures smooth functioning and simple assembly of pumps, which are often at the core of industrial systems, rather than just obtaining a snug fit. Pump reliability and effectiveness could be seriously jeopardized without reaming. 5. Aerospace Reaming is indispensable in aerospace manufacturing, in which precision is non-negotiable. It's employed to form exact fastener holes in critical components like wings and landing gear. This ensures a secure assembly and robust performance of aircraft parts, which are essential for the structural integrity and safety of the aircraft during flight. 6. Bearings Reaming is used to produce precise holes in bearings. These are essential components of many machines and pieces of equipment, and reaming is the process used to create exact holes in them. It ensures that bearings fit snugly and operate smoothly, which is essential for the longevity and reliability of machinery. What Are the Advantages of Reaming? Reaming offers several advantages in manufacturing: High Precision: It produces holes with tight tolerances and excellent surface finishes. Efficiency: Reaming can be performed quickly, enhancing productivity. Versatility: It can be used on a variety of materials and is suitable for both hand and machine operations. Cost-Effective: The tools required for reaming are generally low-cost, and the process can be economical for finishing holes. Surface Finish: Decreasing the feed rate during reaming can improve the surface finish of the hole. What Are the Disadvantages of Reaming? Despite its benefits, reaming also has some disadvantages: Pre-Machined Holes Required: Reaming cannot create a hole; it can only enlarge and finish pre-drilled or pre-machined holes. Tool Wear: If not used correctly, there is a risk of tool breakage and wear. Dimensional Control: There is less control over the dimensions of holes compared to other processes like boring. What Are the Common Problems in Reaming? Some common problems encountered during reaming include: Poor Fit Quality : Reaming tools only follow the existing hole. This can result in poor fit quality if the initial hole is not accurately drilled or if there are deviations in the hole's dimensions. This can lead to scrap parts and rework. Damage to Inserts : Cutting inserts in reaming tools may get damaged, especially if the workpiece material has problems or if the cutting circumstances are not ideal. There could be additional expenses and downtime associated with reconditioning or replacing the inserts due to this damage. Lost Production Time : When reaming tools become damaged and require reconditioning or replacement, it can lead to lost production time. Reconditioning processes can be lengthy, causing delays in production schedules and impacting overall efficiency. What Are the Different Types of Reaming Tools? There are various types of reaming tools , each designed for specific applications: Hand Reamers: Used primarily for manual operations to improve the fitting of parts. Stub Screw-Machine Reamers: These reamers can be identified by a transverse pinhole in the shaft, which allows them to be used in a floating reamer holder. This feature is common in many reamer styles and is particularly useful for applications with shallow holes. Shell Reamers: Designed for reaming large holes and often used in a machine setup. Chucking Straight-Fluted Reamers: Chucking straight-fluted reamers are designed for machine use, featuring straight flutes and a smooth shank for collet or chuck mounting. They're ideal for precise hole finishing, but not suited for hand-reaming due to their straight flute design. Taper Pin Reamers: These have tapered flutes for precision fitting of tapered pins and can have various flute designs. They are categorized by tip diameter, root diameter, and length. Carbide Reamers: Made from hard materials like tungsten-carbide, titanium-carbide, and tantalum-carbide, these reamers are very brittle and must be handled carefully to avoid damage. Diemaker’s Reamers: Diemaker's reamers are characterized by their three flutes cut on a multi-turn helix, making them suitable for rapid cutting. They are especially useful for reaming holes with keyways and oil galleries, in which other tools with shallow-angle or straight flutes might jam. How To Choose a Reamer? When selecting a reamer, consider the material to be reamed, the diameter of the hole, the amount of stock to be removed, and the desired accuracy and finish. What Is the Importance of Choosing a Reamer? Choosing the right reamer is important for precision in traditional and CNC machining. It ensures the hole is accurately sized and has a smooth finish, which is essential for the high levels of precision required in industries like aerospace and automotive manufacturing. How Does the Choice of Reamer Impact the Reaming Result? The choice of reamer significantly affects the reaming result. Using the correct reamer type and size can lead to a high-quality surface finish, superb hole quality, and close dimensional tolerance. So, yes, reamer choice has a major effect. How To Use a Reamer? Using a reamer correctly is essential for achieving the desired precision in machined holes. Here's a step-by-step guide on how to use a reamer: Secure the Workpiece: Ensure that the workpiece is held securely and will not slide or rock during the reaming process. Pre-Drill the Hole: Drill the hole to slightly less than the final diameter. The size of the drill should be chosen based on the reamer size; for reamers up to 1/2", subtract 2% to 4% from the reamer diameter. Apply Lubricant: If necessary, apply a light-cutting oil or coolant to the material to facilitate smoother cutting and prolong the life of the reamer. Insert the Reamer: Place the reamer into the hole. If using a hand reamer, ensure it is properly aligned with the hole's axis. Ream the Hole: Turn the reamer with steady pressure. For machine reaming, use the machine's feed mechanism. For hand reaming, use a tap wrench or similar tool to turn the reamer. Avoid applying excessive force, which can lead to oversizing the hole or damaging the reamer. Check the Size: Regularly check the hole size during the reaming process to ensure that the desired diameter is achieved. When To Use a Reamer? Reamers are useful for: achieving exact hole diameters, clean surfaces, and the removal of burrs and defects from prior machining operations. What Are the Materials That Are Suited for Reaming? Reaming is suited for a variety of materials, including: plastics, metals, and composites. The reamer construction can be from high-speed steel (HSS), cobalt alloys, or carbide materials. What Are Tips for Using a Reamer? When using a reamer, it's important to follow best practices to ensure the best results. Here are some tips: Use the Right Cutting Fluid or Lubricant: Proper lubrication can reduce friction and heat, leading to a better finish and longer tool life. Maintain Proper Speed and Feed Rate: Adhere to recommended speeds and feeds to prevent tool wear and achieve the desired surface finish. Apply Consistent Pressure: Even and steady pressure ensures uniform cutting and prevents irregularities in the hole's finish. Check Hole Sizing Regularly: Frequent checks can prevent over-reaming and ensure that the hole dimensions remain within the desired tolerances. Deburring and Cleaning: After reaming, remove any burrs and clean the hole to ensure a smooth finish. Practice and Gain Experience: Like any skill, proficiency with reaming comes with practice, so take the time to learn and improve. Is Reaming Hard? No, reaming is not considered a heavy-cutting operation and is generally more stable and faster than boring and grinding. Will a Reamer Straighten a Hole? Yes, a reamer can straighten a bored hole to very fine tolerances and shape conical holes. What Is the Difference Between Reaming and Boring? Reaming is used to refine the interior walls of an existing hole for a smoother finish and precise size. Compared to reaming, boring can create larger hole sizes and is used to enlarge holes. Very rewarding and highly recommended Engineer 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish.
This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. Very rewarding and highly recommended Engineer 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish.
This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room.
Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design.
Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish.
This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. Very rewarding and highly recommended Engineer 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design. Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. Very rewarding and highly recommended Engineer 01.PPE - Pre Production Engineering Customer supplied data (gerber) is used to produce the manufacturing data for the specific PCB (artworks for imaging processes and drill data for drilling programs). Engineers compare demands/specifications against capabilities to ensure compliance and also determine the process steps and associated checks. No changes are allowed without PCBWay Group permission. 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design. Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport. Artwork Master – The photographic image of the PCB pattern on film used to produce the circuit board, usually on a 1:1 scale.In general, there are three types of Artwork Master:(1) Conductive Pattern (2) solder mask (3) Silkscreen Put away 02.Board Cutting (Copper Clad Laminate Cutting) PCB production starts with a large piece of sheet material. Due to the limitations of PCB production equipment and manufacture capabilities, the factory has requirements for its minimum and maximum processing size. Therefore, under the guidance of manufacture instruction (MI), the raw material of PCB (Copper Clad Laminate ) needs to be cut into the processing size by automatic cutting machine before production. Hide Details 03.Print inner layers Stage 1 is to transfer the image using an artwork film to the board surface, using photosensitive dry-film and UV light, which will polymerise the dry film exposed by the artwork. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. Imaging – The process of transferring electronic data to the photo-plotter, which in turn uses light to transfer a negative image circuitry pattern onto the panel or film. Hide Details 04.Etch inner layers Stage 2 is to remove the unwanted copper from the panel using etching. Once this copper has been removed, the remaining dry film is then removed leaving behind the copper circuitry that matches the design. Etching – The chemical, or chemical and electrolytic, removal of unwanted portions of conductive or resistive material. Hide Details 05.Inner layer Automatic Optical Inspection(AOI) Inspection of the circuitry against digital “images” to verify that the circuitry matches the design and that it is free from defects. Achieved through scanning of the board and then trained inspectors will verify any anomalies that the scanning process has highlighted. PCBWay Group allows no repair of open circuits. Hide Details 06.Lay-up and bond (Lamination) The inner layers have an oxide layer applied and then “stacked” together with pre-preg providing insulation between layers and copper foil is added to the top and bottom of the stack. The lamination process consists of placing the internal layers under extreme temperature (375 degrees Fahrenheit) and pressure (275 to 400 psi) while laminating with a photosensitive dry resist. The PCB is allowed to cure at a high temperature, the pressure is slowly released and then the material is slowly cooled. Hide Details 07.Drilling the PCB We now have to drill the holes that will subsequently create electrical connections within the multilayer PCB. This is a mechanical drilling process that must be optimised so that we can achieve registration to all of the the inner layer connections. The panels can be stacked at this process. The drilling can also be done by a laser drill Hide Details 08.Electroless copper deposition The first step in the plating process is the chemical deposition of a very thin layer of copper on the hole walls. PTH provides a very thin deposit of copper that covers the hole wall and the complete panel. A complex chemical process that must be strictly controlled to allow a reliable deposit of copper to be plated even onto the non-metallic hole wall. Whilst not a sufficient amount of copper on its own, we now have electrical continuity between layers and through the holes.Panel plating follows on from PTH to provide a thicker deposit of copper on top of the PTH deposit – typically 5 to 8 um. The combination is used to optimise the amount of copper that is to be plated and etched in order to achieve the track and gap demands. Hide Details 09.Image the outer layers Similar to the inner layer process (image transfer using photosensitive dry film, exposure to UV light and etching), but with one main difference – we will remove the dry film where we want to keep the copper/define circuitry – so we can plate additional copper later in the process. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. Hide Details 10.Plating Second electrolytic plating stage, where the additional plating is deposited in areas without dry film (circuitry). Once the copper has been plated, tin is applied to protect the plated copper. Hide Details 11.Etch outer layer This is normally a three step process. The first step is to remove the blue dry film. The second step is to etch away the exposed/unwanted copper whilst the tin deposit acts an etch resist protecting the copper we need. The third and final step is to chemically remove the tin deposit leaving the circuitry. Hide Details 12.Outer layer AOI Just like with inner layer AOI the imaged and etched panel is scanned to make sure that the circuitry meets design and that it is free from defects. Again no repair of open circuits are allowed under PCBWay demands. Hide Details 13.Soldermask Soldermask ink is applied over the whole PCB surface. Using artworks and UV light we expose certain areas to the UV and those areas not exposed are removed during the chemical development process – typically the areas which are to be used as solderable surfaces. The remaining soldermask is then fully cured making it a resilient finish. This step of the process is performed in a clean room. Hide Details 14.Surface finish Various finishes are then applied to the exposed copper areas. This is to enable protection of the surface and good solderability. The various finishes can include Electroless Nickel Immersion Gold, HASL, Immersion Silver etc. Thicknesses and solderability tests are always carried out. Hide Details 15.Profile This is the process of cutting the manufac-turing panels into specific sizes and shapes based upon the customer design as defined within the gerber data. There are 3 main options available when providing the array or selling panel – scoring, routing or punching. All dimensions are measured against the customer supplied drawing to ensure the panel is dimensionally correct. Hide Details 16.Electrical test Used for checking the integrity of the tracks and the through hole interconnections – checking to ensure there are no open circuits or no short circuits on the finished board. There are three test methods, flying probe for smaller volumes,fixture based for volumes and 4-wire Kelvin testing (For PCBs use in automotive, or aerospace applications).We electrically test every PCB against the original board data. Using a flying probe tester we check each net to ensure that it is complete (no open circuits) and does not short to any other net. Hide Details 17.Final inspection In the last step of the process a team of sharp-eyed inspectors give each PCB a final careful check-over.Visual checking the PCB against acceptance criteria and using PCBWay “approved” inspectors. Using manual visual inspection and AVI – compares PCB to gerber and has a faster checking speed that human eyes, but still requires human verification. All orders are also subjected to a full inspection including dimensional, solderability, etc. Hide Details 18.Packaging Boards are wrapped using materials that comply with the PCBWay Packaging demands (ESD etcetera) and then boxed prior to be being shipped using the requested mode of transport.
